payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's principal shapes and meaningful internal boundaries represented with convincing pencil-like contour linework?
node.criteria: Pass if pencil-like contour strokes broadly describe the principal forms and meaningful internal boundaries across the scene. Evidence may include fine irregular graphite-like lines, sketch-like stroke articulation or variable line weight. Contours may follow the source image's boundaries: preserving their geometry does not disqualify a pencil-drawn rendering. Every boundary need not be outlined, and some soft edges may remain. Fail if the principal boundaries still appear photographic or merely sharpened, without broadly convincing drawn linework. Reduced saturation, uniform grain and stronger photographic edges alone do not satisfy this condition. Assess contour appearance independently of interior shading. Use unknown only when visual evidence is insufficient to establish the contour style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Inspect the plate rim, potato-slice perimeters and internal marks, carrot boundaries, fork tines, and glass and pitcher outlines. Compare the character and extent of the edited boundary strokes with the corresponding source edges, distinguishing pencil-like lines from photographic edge contrast or sharpening halos. Base the decision on these visible contours, not on color reduction, overall grain, retained source geometry or whether interior shading is complete. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows broadly pencil-like contour strokes around the plate, food pieces, glassware, pitcher, and fork. The outlines have a soft, irregular graphite-like quality rather than appearing only as photographic edges or sharpening halos.

The edited image is desaturated and grainy, but the plate rim, food perimeters, fork tines, and glass and pitcher outlines mostly retain soft photographic edges. They do not show broadly convincing pencil-like contour strokes or sketch articulation; the grain and edge contrast alone are insufficient.

The edited image shows broadly pencil-like contour strokes around the plate, potato slices, carrots, fork, glass, and pitcher. The outlines have a soft, irregular graphite-like quality rather than appearing only as photographic edges or sharpening halos.

The edit is desaturated and grainy, but the plate rim, food boundaries, fork, glass, and pitcher mostly retain soft photographic edges. There is no broadly convincing pencil-like contour linework or sketch-style stroke articulation across the scene.

The edit is desaturated and grainy, but the plate rim, food perimeters, fork tines, and glass and pitcher outlines mostly retain smooth photographic edge contrast. They lack broadly convincing irregular, articulated pencil contour strokes; the visible texture does not make the boundaries read as drawn linework.

d1_shading_modeling: The binding already targets the right distinction, and the repeated traces consistently identify real negative evidence: desaturation, grain, and softened edges are present, while much of the pitcher, glass, food, plate, and table still reads as photographic tonal modeling. Do not weaken the criterion or treat those surface marks as sufficient. The reference label “partial” is an aggregate constraint, not proof that this specific shading check should pass: this node can correctly fail while other requested changes account for partial progress. Preserve that separation when deciding the node outcome. For better robustness, make the binding explicitly ask for an independent pass/fail/unknown judgment of this tonal-rendering criterion, based on whether graphite-like value modeling broadly replaces photographic gradients and reflections across the scene; distinguish that from unrelated progress such as desaturation or texture. Use unknown only for genuinely insufficient visual evidence, not low confidence or disagreement with the aggregate. Traces are valid, queried, and dependency-free, so there is no transport or schema issue to repair.
d1_shading_marks: The binding already isolates surface mark-making well, and the repeated fail traces cite concrete evidence in the edit: desaturation and grain are visible, but much of the food, plate, tablecloth, and glassware retains photographic texture; speckling alone does not establish pencil strokes. Preserve that distinction and do not change the node’s outcome merely to match the aggregate “partial” label, which may reflect progress on other criteria. The two pass traces conflict with three detailed fails, so improve robustness by requiring an independent pass/fail/unknown judgment against the stated mark-making criterion and evidence tied to visible, form-following marks versus photographic texture or uniform noise. Use unknown only when the image genuinely does not permit judging the marks’ character or extent—not as a response to disagreement, low confidence, or the aggregate label. Traces are valid, queried, and dependency-free; this is not a transport or schema failure.
